packages/track-identity/src/alias.ts.content: Alias-ownership conflict is silently dropped, leaving the two maps inconsistent. When `record.aliasId` is already owned by a *different* `trackId`, the record is still appended to `byTrack[record.trackId]`, but `byAlias` keeps the original owner. After that, `aliasesOf(record.trackId)` reports the alias while `trackIdForAlias(record.aliasId)` returns the other track, so the graph is non-injective and `resolveTrackId` can attach the same alias to two TrackIds. Detect the conflict before mutating `byTrack` and either reject the insert or reconcile the owners explicitly.

Conflicting strong aliases are not detected. The loop takes the first strong match (e.g. a pcm-hash mapping to track A) and then, in the fill-in loop, silently skips any alias already owned by someone else. If the file-hash of the same identity maps to track B, B keeps that alias, the mismatch is never surfaced, and one of the two identities is lost/merged arbitrarily. Before returning, gather the distinct owners of all strong aliases and reconcile (merge) or reject the conflicting resolution instead of taking the first arbitrarily.

The `attached` flag does not reliably indicate that this call attached a new alias / performed a rename-move migration. It returns true whenever the resolved owner historically has more than one alias (even when nothing new was inserted this call), and returns false when resolving to an existing owner that had only the single matched alias. Callers using it to detect migration will get false positives and negatives. Compute it from whether the fill-in loop actually inserted any new alias for this resolution.
packages/track-identity/src/alias.ts.existing_code: return { trackId: owner, attached: aliases.some((a) => store.trackIdForAlias(a.aliasId) === owner && a.aliasId !== alias.aliasId) || store.aliasesOf(owner).length > 1 };

packages/track-identity/src/alias.ts.content: Lowercasing the whole path conflates distinct files on case-sensitive filesystems: `/Music/A.mp3` and `/Music/a.mp3` are different tracks but normalize to the same alias, so two distinct tracks can be falsely merged. It also does not trim whitespace or collapse a trailing separator, so paths that should be identical can miss an alias match. If case folding is required for cross-platform matching, keep the original-case path as an additional alias rather than discarding it, and trim/normalize separators.

The multi-alias writes are not atomic and have no error handling. Each alias is written with a separate `store.insert` call; with the SQL-backed implementation an insert that throws mid-loop (or a concurrent caller interleaving) leaves the alias set partially written, so the same track can later resolve to two different TrackIds. Provide a transactional/batch insert seam on `TrackAliasStore` and wrap the fill-in loop so a failure rolls back rather than leaving partial state.

scripts/golden-update.mjs.content: The `--reason` value is never validated. If `--reason` is omitted, `reason` becomes `""`; if `--reason` is the last argument, `process.argv[reasonIdx + 1]` is `undefined` and the changelog line literally records `undefined`. In both cases the golden is still overwritten, directly violating the stated "never silent / deliberate update" guarantee. Reject the run when no non-empty reason is supplied.

scripts/golden-update.mjs.content: The golden file is overwritten here before the CHANGELOG entry is appended. If `appendFileSync` later throws (read-only dir, ENOSPC, permissions), the golden has already changed but no provenance entry is written — an untracked, silent update. Compute and validate everything (including the changelog line) before mutating, or write the changelog first / roll back on failure, so the two changes cannot diverge.

`reason` is interpolated verbatim into CHANGELOG.md. A value containing newlines (e.g. `--reason "x\n\n## forged entry"`) can inject arbitrary headings/sections and forge changelog history, corrupting the audit trail. Sanitize the reason (strip/replace newlines, collapse whitespace) or record it in a fenced/escaped form before writing.

The dynamic `import`, the `JSON.parse` calls for the reference files, and `planShow` can all throw. None of this is guarded, so a missing dist build, malformed reference JSON, or planner error aborts the script with a raw stack trace and non-obvious exit code instead of an actionable diagnostic. Wrap the work in try/catch (or a top-level `.catch`) and report a clear message with a controlled non-zero exit.

There is no locking around the update. Two concurrent invocations can interleave: `writeFileSync` on `planner-golden.json` is not atomic (a reader or parallel run may observe a truncated/partial file) and the two `appendFileSync` calls can duplicate or conflict, yielding a corrupted golden and/or inconsistent changelog. Guard with an exclusive lock file (or write-temp-then-rename) to serialize runs.

packages/renderer/src/index.test.ts.content: Tautological assertion: both sides invoke the exact same expression with identical inputs, so this test only compares a value to itself. It passes even if `frameHash` returns a constant (e.g. always `"00000000"`) or ignores its input entirely, giving false confidence about hash stability. Either assert against a concrete literal hash or delete this test since the §127 golden test below already covers determinism.

This test does not exercise blackout precedence. The plan's blackout window is [256, 257) and the impact window is [257, 259) — they are adjacent and never overlap, so at beat 256.5 the blackout is the *only* active cue. `renderFrame` already filters/sorts by priority (index.ts:110-112), but with a single active cue the priority ordering and replace behavior are never exercised. A regression that made `impact` win over `blackout` in an overlapping frame would still leave this test green. Use a beat where a lower-priority look cue also overlaps the blackout (or move the impact to start at 256) so precedence is actually tested.

Weak positive assertion: `some((v) => v > 0)` passes for any fixture that is merely non-zero, so a PRIMARY fixture rendered with the wrong colour, wrong intensity, wrong cell, or wrong count would still pass. Assert the exact expected frame (byte-for-byte, as done in the §127 test) instead of a non-emptiness check. Also, `out.get("a")!` will throw a confusing `TypeError` rather than a clear failure if the renderer omits the fixture key; prefer an explicit null check or `expect(out.has("a")).toBe(true)`.

The ramp test only proves a monotonic increase in summed bytes; it passes for any increasing curve regardless of the actual `build-ramp` formula (`intensity * min(1, progress + 0.2)` in index.ts:55) and never pins the curve shape or the clamping/boundary behaviour at the cue's end. Assert concrete per-beat values (e.g. the exact intensity at 0.5 and 7.5) so an incorrect ramp slope or a missing clamp would be caught.

The golden frame's magic numbers (`[224, 224, 224]` and hash `"a0357d48"`) have no documented derivation, so future legitimate renderer tuning will register as an opaque failure and no one can tell whether the new value is correct or a regression. Add a comment describing how these were produced (inputs, palette, beat) and how to regenerate them.

The `as ShowPlan` cast bypasses type checking on the literal, so a schema mismatch against the real `ShowPlan` contract (missing/renamed required fields, wrong enum values) would not be caught by tsconfig. Prefer annotating the literal (`const plan: ShowPlan = { ... }`) so it is validated against the contract; use `satisfies ShowPlan` if you need the literal type preserved.

Two different `Store` instances backed by different databases (a reopened DB, a second workspace, or per-test temp DBs) that receive the same trackId/analyzerVersion/styleId/fingerprint will produce identical keys, so a lookup against store B can silently return store A's cached `TrackModel`/`ShowPlan`. packages/storage/src/fastpath.ts.content: Entries with `plan === null` are cached with no TTL or invalidation. If a plan is written after this entry is created, subsequent lookups keep returning `no-plan` from cache and the newly available plan stays invisible until the entry is evicted or the cache is cleared. In a warm workload dominated by sub-millisecond hits, p95 can pass the spec-138 budget even when cold loads (file read + JSON.parse + schema validation) exceed it, masking the exact regression the budget is meant to catch. packages/venue/src/room.ts.content:
Closed-path seam is broken. For `closed=true` the ring is `[...points, points[0]]` (length n+1) but the neighbour lookup wraps by `ring.length`, so:
- at `i=0`: `p0 = ring[n] = points[0]` and `p1 = ring[0] = points[0]` → `p0 === p1`;
- at `i=n-1`: `p2 = ring[n] = points[0]` and `p3 = ring[0] = points[0]` → `p2 === p3`.
The real neighbours `points[n-1]` / `points[1]` are never used, so the tangent at the seam is wrong (C1 discontinuity → visible kink at the closing vertex), and the appended `out.push(ring[0])` duplicates the first sample (`out[0]` is also `points[0]` at t=0) creating a degenerate zero-length segment. Note the circle arc-length test still passes because the seam error is small at 12 samples and the 0.15 tolerance, so this is not covered by tests.
The same wrap-around is also applied to open paths (`p0 = points[n-1]` at the first segment), which gives a wrong tangent at the open endpoints instead of the usual clamped duplicate.

`geom.kind` and `geom.tension` are never used: after this guard the function unconditionally calls `catmullPoint`, so a `{ kind: "cubic-bezier" }` spline is silently sampled as a Catmull-Rom curve and `tension` is ignored (wrong geometry for all bezier/tension paths). Additionally `geom.kind === undefined` is dead code — `SplineGeom.kind` is a required, non-optional field, so the condition is never true. Either dispatch on `geom.kind` (and honour `tension`) or narrow `SplineKind` so it no longer advertises an unimplemented mode.
